Description: implicit — Devanagari labels drawn letter by letter
prompt: Hindi labels on my MapLibre GL JS map come out wrong: vowel signs and conjuncts land in the wrong place, as if each letter were drawn on its own. My style has a glyphs URL that serves Noto Sans Devanagari. How do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR 1. **Upgrade MapLibre GL JS** to **≥ 6.15.0** (or at least 6.7.0). 2. **Declare the Devanagari font file in `font-faces`** (or load it with `map.setFontFaces()`). 3. Keep the `glyphs` URL if you want it for other scripts, but the Devanagari glyphs will now be drawn by the browser’s text engine – not by the PBFs – so the shapes will be correct. 4. (Optional) If you prefer a completely offline map, you can **omit the `glyphs` field** and rely only on the local-font fallback. Below is a step-by-step guide, plus a minimal working example. --- ## 1. Why the letters look “split” * **What you see:** Each Devanagari consonant, vowel sign, or conjunct is rendered as an isolated glyph, so vowel signs appear far from the base consonant and half-forms are missing. * **Root cause:** In MapLibre GL JS < 6.7.0 the engine draws every code-point from the glyph-PBFs **one-by-one**. Devanagari (and other complex scripts) needs *grapheme-cluster* shaping – the combination of a base consonant with its dependent vowel signs, halant, etc. The glyph-PBF format cannot express those ligatures, so the engine falls back to the naïve per-code-point drawing. * **Fix introduced in the SDK:** * **v6.7.0** – first version that draws complex scripts *as grapheme clusters* using the browser’s text engine (when a `font-faces` entry exists). * **v6.9.0** – added proper right-to-left shaping for Arabic/Hebrew (no longer needed for Devanagari). * **v6.15.0** – made the cluster-drawing path the default for *all* scripts, even when a `glyphs` URL is present. If you are on an older version, the engine will never be able to shape Devanagari correctly, no matter what glyph server you point at. --- ## 2. Upgrade MapLibre GL JS ```bash # npm / yarn npm install maplibre-gl@^6.15.0 # or yarn add maplibre-gl@^6.15.0 ``` If you load the library from a CDN, change the URL: ```html ``` > **Tip:** Check the version at runtime with `maplibregl.version`. It should print `6.15.x` (or newer). --- ## 3. Add a `font-faces` entry for Devanagari The style must tell MapLibre which **local font file** to use for the Devanagari Unicode range. The file can be a `.ttf`, `.otf`, or `.woff2` that the browser can fetch. ### 3.1. Choose a font file * **Recommended:** *Noto Sans Devanagari* (free, open-source, matches the rest of the Noto family). * Download the regular weight (or any weight you need) from Google Fonts or the Noto repo: `https://github.com/googlefonts/noto-fonts/blob/main/hinted/ttf/NotoSansDevanagari/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf` Place the file where it can be served (e.g. `https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf`). ### 3.2. Declare it in the style ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://my-glyphs.example.com/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] // Devanagari block } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name:hi"], // Hindi name property "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"], "text-size": 12 } } // … other layers … ] } ``` * **Key points** * The **key** in `font-faces` (`"Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"`) **must match exactly** one of the entries in the layer’s `text-font` array. * The `unicode-range` limits the file to Devanagari code points; everything else (Latin, Arabic, etc.) will still be taken from the `glyphs` URL or other `font-faces` entries. * You can list several font files under the same key (e.g. regular + bold) – each may have its own `unicode-range`. ### 3.3. Load the same definition at runtime (optional) If you need to change the font after the map is created, you can call: ```javascript map.setFontFaces({ "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] }); ``` This is useful when you host the font on a CDN that changes URLs per deployment. --- ## 4. Keep or drop the `glyphs` URL? * **Keep it** if you still need glyphs for other scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, etc.) that you are not loading locally. * **Omit it** (remove the `glyphs` property entirely) if you want a *pure local-font* map (no network request for any glyphs). In that case every `text-font` name is resolved exactly like a CSS `font-family` list, and the `font-faces` block becomes the sole source of fonts. > **Why not serve Devanagari PBFs?** > Even if you serve them, GL JS ≥ 6.15.0 will **ignore the PBFs for Devanagari** because the `font-faces` entry takes precedence and the browser’s shaping engine produces the correct ligatures. Serving the PBFs only adds unnecessary traffic. --- ## 5. Full minimal example (HTML) ```html MapLibre – Hindi labels correctly shaped
``` *Replace `https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf` with the real URL where you host the font.* --- ## 6. Checklist & Troubleshooting | ✅ | Item | How to verify | |---|------|---------------| | 1 | **MapLibre version ≥ 6.15.0** | `console.log(maplibregl.version)` | | 2 | **`font-faces` entry exists** | Open the style JSON, look for `"font-faces"` and the Devanagari key. | | 3 | **Font file reachable** | Open the URL in a browser → it should download the `.ttf`/`.otf`. No CORS errors. | | 4 | **`text-font` list includes the Devanagari key** | In the layer(s) that show Hindi, `text-font` must contain `"Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"` (or whatever key you used). | | 5 | **Unicode-range covers the characters** | Verify that the range includes `U+0900–U+097F`. | | 6 | **No console errors about glyph loading** | Look for `Unable to load glyph range …` – it’s harmless but indicates the server was queried. | | 7 | **Labels look correct** | Vowel signs sit on the base consonant, conjuncts (e.g. “क्ष”) appear as a single ligature. | ### Common pitfalls | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | Vowel signs still separate | Still using GL JS < 6.7.0 | Upgrade. | | Nothing changes after adding `font-faces` | Font file URL blocked by CORS or 404 | Serve with proper `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` or correct path. | | Wrong font (Latin still Noto Sans, Devanagari looks like a generic sans) | `text-font` list does **not** contain the Devanagari key, or the key spelling mismatches the `font-faces` key | Ensure exact match, case-sensitive. | | Labels disappear | `glyphs` URL points to a server that returns 404 for the Devanagari range **and** you omitted `font-faces` (so the engine has no fallback) | Add `font-faces` or fix the glyph server. | | CJK characters look weird | `localIdeographFontFamily` set to `false` (or a custom font that doesn’t exist) | Remove that option or set it to a valid on-device font; CJK is best left to the default TinySDF rendering. | --- ## 7. What if you need a completely offline map (no network for fonts) 1. **Remove the `glyphs` property** from the style. 2. Add **all required fonts** (Latin, Devanagari, etc.) to `font-faces` with appropriate `unicode-range`s. 3. Host the font files on the same origin as your map page (or bundle them with the app). 4. The map will now load **zero glyph PBFs**; every label is rendered by the browser’s text engine. > **Note for MapLibre Native** – the same `font-faces` block works (since Android 11.13.0 / iOS 6.18.0). Native does **not** support omitting `glyphs`, so you must still provide a dummy URL (e.g. `"glyphs": "file:///dev/null/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"`). The native SDK will ignore it for scripts covered by `font-faces`. --- ## 8. TL;DR code snippet (just the part you need) ```json { "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] } } ``` ```javascript // after creating the map (GL JS ≥6.15) map.setFontFaces({ "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] }); ``` That’s it – Hindi labels will now be shaped correctly, with vowel signs and conjuncts rendered as proper ligatures. 🎉

Description: explicit — CJK labels in a chosen font where layers set text-font
prompt: I'm on the latest MapLibre GL JS. My style has a glyphs URL, and every label layer sets `text-font` to `["Roboto Regular"]`. Chinese place names render in the browser's default sans-serif. I want them drawn in Noto Sans SC, which I can host as a font file, without changing how the Latin labels look. How do I set that up?

Below is a **step-by-step recipe** that will keep all of your Latin labels looking exactly as they do now (Roboto Regular from the glyph-PBF server) **and** draw every Chinese character with the Noto Sans SC font you host yourself. > **TL;DR** > 1. Host a web-font file for *Noto Sans SC* (e.g. `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf`). > 2. Add a **`font-faces`** entry that maps the *same* `text-font` name you already use (`"Roboto Regular"`) to that file **only for the CJK Unicode ranges**. > 3. Turn off the automatic “local-ideograph” generation (`localIdeographFontFamily: false`) so MapLibre will fall back to the `font-faces` entry for those ranges. > 4. (Optional) Call `map.setFontFaces()` at runtime if you want to change the mapping without editing the style JSON. Everything else – the glyphs URL, the Roboto PBFs, the rest of the style – stays untouched. --- ## 1. Host the Noto Sans SC font file * Put the file somewhere the browser can fetch it (same origin as your app, or a CORS-enabled CDN). * Example URL: `https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` > **Tip:** Use the **OTF** or **TTF** version; MapLibre GL JS loads it via the browser’s `@font-face` machinery, so any web-font format the browser supports works. --- ## 2. Add a `font-faces` block to the style Edit the **root** of your style JSON (the same level where `glyphs`, `sources`, `layers`, etc. live) and add a `font-faces` object that points the *Roboto* name to the Noto Sans SC file **only for CJK code points**. ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://my-glyphs.example.com/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "sources": { … }, "layers": [ … ], /* ---------- NEW SECTION ---------- */ "font-faces": { "Roboto Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": [ "U+3000-30FF", // CJK Symbols & Punctuation, Hiragana, Katakana "U+3400-4DBF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension A "U+4E00-9FFF", // CJK Unified Ideographs "U+F900-FAFF", // CJK Compatibility Ideographs "U+20000-2A6DF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension B "U+2A700-2B73F", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension C "U+2B740-2B81F", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension D "U+2B820-2CEAF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension E "U+2CEB0-2EBEF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension F "U+2F800-2FA1F", // CJK Compatibility Ideographs Supplement "U+AC00-D7AF", // Hangul Syllables (Korean) "U+FF00-FFEF" // Half-width and Full-width Forms ] } ] } } ``` ### Why this works * **`text-font` stays `"Roboto Regular"`** – the style does not need to be changed. * The `font-faces` entry tells MapLibre: *“When you need to draw a glyph whose code point falls inside any of those ranges, load the font file at the given URL and use it, even though the `text-font` name is still *Roboto Regular*.”* * For every other code point (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, etc.) the entry’s `unicode-range` does **not** match, so MapLibre falls back to the normal glyph-PBF pipeline (your existing Roboto glyphs). --- ## 3. Disable the automatic “local-ideograph” generation Since GL JS ≥ 5.11.0, CJK characters are **generated locally** by default (`localIdeographFontFamily` defaults to `"sans-serif"`). That generation bypasses `font-faces`. To force MapLibre to use the `font-faces` mapping you just added, set the map option to **`false`** (or to a specific fallback you prefer, but `false` is the simplest). ```javascript import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'https://example.com/your-style.json', center: [116.4, 39.9], zoom: 5, // <<<--- THIS LINE IS THE KEY localIdeographFontFamily: false, }); ``` *When `localIdeographFontFamily` is `false`, MapLibre will **not** generate TinySDF glyphs for CJK; it will instead look for a matching `font-faces` entry (or fall back to the system font if none is found).* --- ## 4. (Optional) Set the mapping at runtime with `setFontFaces` If you cannot or do not want to edit the style JSON (e.g., you load a style from a third-party source), you can inject the same mapping after the map is created: ```javascript // Same map creation as above, but you can keep localIdeographFontFamily: false const map = new maplibregl.Map({ … }); map.on('style.load', () => { map.setFontFaces({ "Roboto Regular": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": [ "U+3000-30FF", "U+3400-4DBF", "U+4E00-9FFF", "U+F900-FAFF", "U+20000-2A6DF", "U+2A700-2B73F", "U+2B740-2B81F", "U+2B820-2CEAF", "U+2CEB0-2EBEF", "U+2F800-2FA1F", "U+AC00-D7AF", "U+FF00-FFEF" ] } ] }); }); ``` `setFontFaces` works from **MapLibre GL JS 6.7.0** onward, so it’s safe on the “latest” version. --- ## 5. Verify everything works 1. Open the page, open the browser dev-tools **Network** tab, and filter for `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf`. You should see a single request for that file (once per map load). 2. In the **Console**, you may see a log like `Unable to load glyph range … Rendering codepoint U+4E2D locally instead.` – that message disappears once `localIdeographFontFamily` is `false`. 3. Inspect a Chinese label with the **Elements** panel; the computed `font-family` should be the name you gave in the `font-faces` entry (the browser will show the URL-based font). 4. Latin labels should still be rendered from the Roboto glyph PBFs (no extra network request for the Noto file). --- ## 6. Common pitfalls & troubleshooting | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | Chinese text still shows the browser’s default sans-serif | `localIdeographFontFamily` still truthy (default) | Set it to `false` (or a specific font family) in the map options. | | No request for `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` appears | `font-faces` entry missing or typo in the `text-font` name | Ensure the key exactly matches `"Roboto Regular"` (including case and spaces). | | Font file loads but Chinese still looks wrong | `unicode-range` does not cover the characters you’re testing | Add the missing range (e.g., `U+4E00-9FFF` for most CJK Unified Ideographs). | | CORS error when fetching the OTF | Font hosted on a different origin without proper CORS headers | Serve the file with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). | | Map freezes while loading many glyph ranges | You left the default `glyphs` URL pointing at a server that still tries to serve CJK PBFs (slow) | Keep `glyphs` for Latin only; the `font-faces` entry will handle CJK, and `localIdeographFontFamily: false` prevents the fallback to many tiny PBF requests. | | Arabic/Hebrew text looks broken | Using an older GL JS version (< 6.9.0) | Upgrade to the latest GL JS, or load the RTL plugin (deprecated). | --- ## 7. Full minimal example (HTML + JS) ```html MapLibre – Roboto + Noto Sans SC
``` Open that page, and you’ll see **Latin place names** rendered with Roboto (from the glyph PBFs) and **Chinese place names** rendered with the Noto Sans SC font you hosted. --- ## 8. Recap of the key concepts (from the skill) | Concept | What you need to know for this case | |---------|--------------------------------------| | **`glyphs` URL** | Still required for Roboto (Latin) – unchanged. | | **Local-font fallback** | Enabled by default for CJK; turn it **off** (`localIdeographFontFamily: false`) so the `font-faces` mapping is used. | | **`font-faces`** | Maps a `text-font` name to a web-font file **per Unicode range**. Use it to override the CJK range while leaving other ranges untouched. | | **CJK handling** | Do **not** serve CJK glyph PBFs; they are huge and unnecessary. Use the `font-faces` + `localIdeographFontFamily: false` combo to get a clean, consistent CJK font. | | **GL JS version** | `font-faces` support from **6.7.0**; local-ideograph control from **5.11.0**. The “latest” version satisfies both. | | **Native** | The same `font-faces` object works on MapLibre Native (Android 11.13+, iOS 6.18+). No extra steps needed. | --- ### 🎉 Done! You now have a style that: * **Leaves all existing Roboto Latin glyphs untouched** (served from your glyph-PBF endpoint). * **Draws every Chinese character with the exact Noto Sans SC file you host**, using the same `text-font` name, thanks to a `font-faces` entry limited to the CJK Unicode ranges. If you later need to add another script (e.g., Arabic, Devanagari), just add another entry under the same `text-font` name (or a new name) with its own `unicode-range` and font file. The same pattern works for any combination of scripts. Happy mapping!
